title: Each according to strength (Exodus Rabbah 5:9)
hook: each person at Sinai heard the voice according to their own strength
tomorrow: why give the Torah in a desert, of all places?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world held its breath: no bird, no ox, no sea, no angel, and one voice into the stillness. But one voice, a whole people listening. Did they all hear the same thing?
screen: `THE WORLD HELD ITS BREATH.` → `ONE VOICE, A WHOLE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: One message in the group chat, and eleven different reactions. A coach says pick it up, and one player runs harder while another goes home and can't sleep. Same words, different people. An aunt asks are you eating enough, and one cousin hears love while another hears an attack. Anyone who has given feedback, or gotten it, knows this week's version. A midrash in Exodus Rabbah asks it about Sinai, and its answer is a gift for anyone who has to say something hard.
screen: `ONE MESSAGE, ELEVEN REACTIONS.` → `SAME WORDS, DIFFERENT PEOPLE.` → `THE SINAI VERSION.`

segments.voice: The midrash starts from a line in the Psalms: "The voice of the LORD is powerful." In Hebrew, ba-koach, with strength. And it notices what the verse doesn't say. Not with His strength. Just with strength. So whose strength? Each listener's. The voice went out to every person according to their own strength: the elders by theirs, the young by theirs, the children by theirs, even the babies by theirs. One voice, and no one got more than they could carry, or less. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight: a whole teaching about how God speaks, built on a missing pronoun. Now bring it into this week. When you have something hard to say, a note to a teammate, bad news to a parent, a correction to a friend, the midrash suggests the message can stay the same while the delivery fits the person. That isn't playing favorites. The Passover table does something like it every year, with four children who each get the story in their own way. And it's how the one voice at Sinai worked. And it runs the other way, too. If you hear old words differently from your grandmother, or your friend gets something out of a prayer that you don't, that may be the voice reaching each of you at your own strength.
screen: `WITH STRENGTH. WHOSE?` · `EACH LISTENER'S OWN.` · `SAME MESSAGE, FITTED DELIVERY.` · `YOUR WAY OF HEARING COUNTS.` · then, large: `EACH ACCORDING TO STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Say the psalm's line out loud three ways: in a whisper, in your ordinary voice, and slowly, one word at a time. The voice of the LORD is powerful. Notice which way reaches you today, then rest in the quiet and let that one echo.
screen: `A WHISPER.` · `YOUR ORDINARY VOICE.` · `SLOWLY.` · `WHICH ONE REACHES YOU?`

segments.voice: Each according to strength: the midrash's reading of Psalm twenty-nine. The voice at Sinai reached each person, old or young, at the strength they could bear.
Carry this: each according to strength. One voice, sized to every listener, so nobody was left out.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching often speaks of explaining the Torah to each learner at their own level, as the Passover Haggadah does with its four children; this midrash on Sinai is one of the sources people bring for it.

fork.setup: the family trip is canceled. you have to tell your grandpa, who hates surprises, and your six-year-old cousin. by the midrash, what's the move?

fork.reveal: at Sinai one voice reached each person according to their strength. the message stays the same; the delivery fits the listener.
